summary.text: Factoring off the two low bits reduces the problem to realizing \(Y=n(n+1)\) by \(g(M)=M^2\operatorname{XOR}M(M+1)\); for \(D=n+1\), the congruence \(g(M+2^s)\equiv g(M)+2^s\pmod{2^{s+1}}\) permits a greedy bit-by-bit construction of \(M<2^D\) with \(g(M)\equiv Y\pmod{2^D}\). Since \(Y<2^D\), a carry split makes this congruence exact: without a carry one takes the even candidate \(2M\), while with a carry the complementary value \(2^D-M\) yields a bounded congruent XOR and hence the odd candidate \(2(2^D-M)-1\).

full_proof.text:
We prove that for every natural number \(n\) there is a natural number \(k\) such that
\[
k^2\operatorname{XOR}(k+1)^2=(2n+1)^2.
\]
Here \(\operatorname{XOR}\) denotes bitwise exclusive-or in base 2.

We will use the following elementary facts about binary XOR.

1. If \(Q=2^d\), then reduction modulo \(Q\) simply retains the lowest \(d\) binary digits. Consequently,
\[
(A\operatorname{XOR}B)\bmod Q
 =((A\bmod Q)\operatorname{XOR}(B\bmod Q)).
\]
In particular, congruent inputs modulo \(Q\) give congruent XORs modulo \(Q\).

2. If \(\lfloor A/Q\rfloor=\lfloor B/Q\rfloor\), then \(A\) and \(B\) have identical binary digits in all positions \(d,d+1,\ldots\). Their XOR therefore has no nonzero digit in those positions, and hence
\[
A\operatorname{XOR}B<Q.
\]

3. Appending the two low binary digits \(00\) to one number and \(01\) to another gives
\[
(4A)\operatorname{XOR}(4B+1)=4(A\operatorname{XOR}B)+1.
\]
Indeed, above the lowest two positions the bits are exactly those of \(A\) and \(B\), while the two lowest bits are respectively \(00\) and \(01\).

Define
\[
g(m)=m^2\operatorname{XOR}m(m+1).
\]
We first reduce the original problem to making a suitable value of \(g\), or a closely related XOR, equal to \(n(n+1)\).

If \(k=2m\), then
\[
k^2=4m^2,
\qquad
(k+1)^2=(2m+1)^2=4m(m+1)+1.
\]
By fact 3,
\[
(2m)^2\operatorname{XOR}(2m+1)^2
 =4\bigl(m^2\operatorname{XOR}m(m+1)\bigr)+1
 =4g(m)+1.                                      \tag{1}
\]

Likewise, if \(m\geq 1\) and \(k=2m-1\), then
\[
k^2=(2m-1)^2=4m(m-1)+1,
\qquad
(k+1)^2=(2m)^2=4m^2.
\]
Using fact 3 and commutativity of XOR gives
\[
(2m-1)^2\operatorname{XOR}(2m)^2
 =4\bigl(m^2\operatorname{XOR}m(m-1)\bigr)+1.  \tag{2}
\]
Finally,
\[
(2n+1)^2=4n(n+1)+1.                             \tag{3}
\]
Thus it suffices to produce either an \(m\) with \(g(m)=n(n+1)\), for use in (1), or an \(m\geq1\) with
\[
m^2\operatorname{XOR}m(m-1)=n(n+1),
\]
for use in (2).

Set
\[
Y=n(n+1),\qquad D=n+1,
\qquad Q=2^D.
\]
Two elementary properties of these quantities will be important. First, \(Y\) is even, since one of the consecutive integers \(n,n+1\) is even. Second,
\[
Y=n(n+1)<2^{n+1}=Q.                             \tag{4}
\]
For completeness, the latter inequality follows by induction. It is immediate for the first few values. For the induction step, assume
\(n(n+1)<2^{n+1}\). For \(n\geq2\),
\[
(n+1)(n+2)\leq 2n(n+1)<2\cdot2^{n+1}=2^{n+2};
\]
the first inequality is equivalent to \(n^2-n-2\geq0\). The remaining small induction steps are checked directly. This proves (4).

We next construct \(M<Q\) satisfying
\[
g(M)\equiv Y\pmod Q.                            \tag{5}
\]
The construction is a binary lifting procedure. Its key property is that for every \(s\geq1\),
\[
g(m+2^s)\equiv g(m)+2^s\pmod {2^{s+1}}.        \tag{6}
\]
Let \(P=2^s\), so \(P\) is even. Expanding the two factors gives
\[
(m+P)^2=m^2+2P(m+P/2),
\]
and therefore
\[
(m+P)^2\equiv m^2\pmod{2P}.                    \tag{7}
\]
Similarly,
\[
(m+P)(m+P+1)
 =m(m+1)+P+2P(m+P/2),
\]
so
\[
(m+P)(m+P+1)\equiv m(m+1)+P\pmod{2P}.          \tag{8}
\]
Modulo \(2P=2^{s+1}\), adding \(P=2^s\) toggles precisely the binary digit in position \(s\), leaving all lower digits fixed. Equations (7) and (8), together with the fact that XOR modulo a power of two depends only on the corresponding low bits, show that the low \(s+1\) bits of \(g(m+P)\) are obtained from those of \(g(m)\) by toggling bit \(s\). This is exactly (6).

We now lift from modulus \(2\) to modulus \(Q\). Begin with
\[
m_1=0.
\]
Since \(g(0)=0\) and \(Y\) is even,
\[
g(m_1)\equiv Y\pmod2.
\]
Suppose, for some \(s\geq1\), that \(m_s<2^s\) and
\[
g(m_s)\equiv Y\pmod{2^s}.
\]
There are exactly two residue classes modulo \(2^{s+1}\) lying above any fixed residue class modulo \(2^s\): if the common residue modulo \(2^s\) is \(r\), the two possibilities modulo \(2^{s+1}\) are \(r\) and \(r+2^s\). If already
\[
g(m_s)\equiv Y\pmod{2^{s+1}},
\]
set \(m_{s+1}=m_s\). Otherwise set
\[
m_{s+1}=m_s+2^s.
\]
By (6), the second choice changes the residue of \(g\) modulo \(2^{s+1}\) from one of the two possible lifts to the other, so in the latter case it must agree with \(Y\). In either case,
\[
g(m_{s+1})\equiv Y\pmod{2^{s+1}},
\qquad m_{s+1}<2^{s+1}.
\]
After continuing through \(s=D-1\), we obtain a natural number
\[
M=m_D<Q
\]
with property (5).

It remains to turn congruence (5) into an exact equality. Write
\[
M^2=WQ+R,
\qquad 0\leq R<Q,
\]
so \(R=M^2\bmod Q\). We distinguish whether adding \(M\) to the low residue \(R\) produces a carry across the \(Q\)-boundary.

Case 1: \(R+M<Q\).

Since
\[
M(M+1)=M^2+M=WQ+(R+M)
\]
and \(R+M<Q\), the two numbers \(M^2\) and \(M(M+1)\) have the same quotient \(W\) upon division by \(Q\). By binary fact 2,
\[
g(M)=M^2\operatorname{XOR}M(M+1)<Q.            \tag{9}
\]
We already know from (5) that \(g(M)\equiv Y\pmod Q\), and by (4) both \(g(M)\) and \(Y\) lie in \([0,Q)\). Hence
\[
g(M)=Y.                                        \tag{10}
\]
Take \(k=2M\). Equations (1), (10), and (3) yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
k^2\operatorname{XOR}(k+1)^2
 &=4g(M)+1\\
 &=4Y+1\\
 &=(2n+1)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the desired \(k\) exists in this case.

Case 2: \(R+M\geq Q\).

Define the complementary number
\[
M'=Q-M.
\]
Because \(M<Q\), we have \(1\leq M'\leq Q\). We will prove that
\[
M'^2\operatorname{XOR}M'(M'-1)=Y.               \tag{11}
\]
There are two parts: first a congruence modulo \(Q\), and then a bound showing that this XOR is below \(Q\).

Since \(M'=Q-M\), reduction modulo \(Q\) gives
\[
M'^2\equiv (-M)^2=M^2\pmod Q.                  \tag{12}
\]
Also
\[
M'(M'-1)=(Q-M)(Q-M-1)
 \equiv(-M)(-M-1)=M(M+1)\pmod Q.               \tag{13}
\]
XOR modulo \(Q\) depends only on the low \(D\) bits, so (12) and (13) imply
\[
M'^2\operatorname{XOR}M'(M'-1)
 \equiv M^2\operatorname{XOR}M(M+1)
 =g(M)
 \equiv Y\pmod Q.                               \tag{14}
\]

We now show that the XOR on the left of (14) is less than \(Q\). It is enough, by binary fact 2, to prove that \(M'^2\) and \(M'(M'-1)\) have the same quotient upon division by \(Q\).

Recall that \(M^2=WQ+R\). Direct expansion of \(M'=Q-M\) gives
\[
M'^2+2MQ
 =(Q-M)^2+2MQ
 =Q^2+M^2
 =(Q+W)Q+R.                                     \tag{15}
\]
Because \(0\leq R<Q\), division of (15) by \(Q\) gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{M'^2}{Q}\right\rfloor+2M=Q+W. \tag{16}
\]
For the other product, observe that
\[
M'(M'-1)=M'^2-M'.
\]
Using \(M'=Q-M\) and (15), we get
\[
\begin{aligned}
M'(M'-1)+2MQ
 &=M'^2-(Q-M)+2MQ\\
 &=(Q+W)Q+R-Q+M\\
 &=(Q+W)Q+(R+M-Q).                              \tag{17}
\end{aligned}
\]
The present case assumption says \(R+M-Q\geq0\). Moreover, since both \(R<Q\) and \(M<Q\),
\[
R+M-Q<Q.
\]
Thus \(R+M-Q\) is precisely the remainder in (17), and division by \(Q\) yields
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{M'(M'-1)}{Q}\right\rfloor+2M=Q+W. \tag{18}
\]
Comparing (16) and (18),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{M'^2}{Q}\right\rfloor
 =
\left\lfloor\frac{M'(M'-1)}{Q}\right\rfloor.
\]
Therefore the binary digits of these two numbers at positions \(D\) and above coincide, and hence
\[
M'^2\operatorname{XOR}M'(M'-1)<Q.               \tag{19}
\]
By (4), \(Y<Q\). Combining (14) and (19), both sides of the congruence (14) are in \([0,Q)\), so the congruence is an equality. This proves (11).

Now take
\[
k=2M'-1,
\]
which is a natural number because \(M'\geq1\). By (2), (11), and (3),
\[
\begin{aligned}
k^2\operatorname{XOR}(k+1)^2
 &=4\bigl(M'^2\operatorname{XOR}M'(M'-1)\bigr)+1\\
 &=4Y+1\\
 &=(2n+1)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
This supplies the required \(k\) in the second case as well.

The two cases exhaust all possibilities for \(R+M\). Therefore, for every \(n\geq0\), there exists a natural number \(k\) such that
\[
k^2\operatorname{XOR}(k+1)^2=(2n+1)^2.
\]
Consequently the defining set for A224515 is nonempty for every \(n\), which is exactly the asserted existence conjecture.
